title: We're a team of 4 building a multiplayer browser game with AI, and here's what we've learned so far
author: First_Teach
selftext:
Hey everyone!

We're a small team of four working on a cozy multiplayer browser game called Talewyn Harbor.

When we started, we used AI quite heavily to help us get things moving. From coding and prototyping gameplay systems to generating some of the early visuals, it helped us build something playable much faster than we originally expected.

But as the game grew, we started running into problems.

The biggest ones were inconsistent visuals, character models that didn't always work well together, a UI that felt all over the place, and performance issues. Especially since we're trying to run a multiplayer 3D world directly in the browser.

We also got quite a bit of feedback from players about these things, and a lot of it was fair.

So over the last few weeks, we've been going back and reworking a huge part of the game.

We've redesigned the entire UI, started replacing the original AI-generated models with custom ones, reworked the environments and spent a lot of time improving performance.

We're still using AI to help with development, but we've learned that getting something working with AI and turning it into a polished game are two very different things.

The game itself has fishing, farming, mining, crafting, cooking, boats, homesteads, multiplayer and quite a few other systems already working.

It's been a pretty interesting experience seeing how far AI can take a small team, but also where you really need to step in and rethink things yourself.

If anyone's curious, the game is playable here: [https://talewyn.org](https://talewyn.org/)

I'd actually love to hear from other developers using AI. Have you also reached a point where you had to go back and rebuild parts of your game because the initial AI-assisted approach became difficult to maintain?

We're still figuring things out ourselves, so it'd be interesting to hear how others are handling it.

comments.author: Fair_Simple_8813
comments.body: Which change gave you the biggest performance improvement: replacing the models, reworking the environments, or something in the multiplayer code? Before-and-after numbers from the same scene and player count would be interesting. It'd help separate the visual cleanup from what actually made the browser build run better.

replies.author: First_Teach
replies.body:
https://reddit.com/link/1xmo2ku/video/nh0kky42ddzh1/player

Hello, yes we changed all the modells because first they was always generated by render, so it helped that we maked real modells for the objets, plus the biggest improvement was the WebGPU insted of WebGL, but for strange some players the WebGL is better.. so hard to figure out what is the best :D

replies.author: Fair_Simple_8813
replies.body: Thanks, that explains the renderer options. I'd keep the manual switch for now and include the active renderer, browser version and device in bug reports. Then you could look for patterns in which setups do better with WebGL, rather than picking one default from the average FPS alone. Do the affected players get consistently lower FPS, or occasional big freezes?

replies.author: Nixi999
replies.body:
It is very mixed result, unfortunately we can get very bad results with high ends setups also. I would say overally WebGL was more stable, as long as you had a medium or a high end setup webgl was nice, it was only sturggling on low end configs and laptops. Still the team mostly decided that we will not countinoue to develop future content for webGL as its a bit older technology, we wanted to optimize for webgpu. Here it switched a little the weak configs gained some fps but higher end setups did lose much more. Atm we are putting a lot of work and time into try different technologies and pick the best development platform for the future. 

Threejs is nice if you make somthing simple and easy to run it every device, but we hit a specific point where we feel this will not be enough for us. I personally want this game to run atleast 60 fps on a lower end PC and 120+ fps on a medium config. So we are not stopping until we get there. Even if it will mean something new like , webassembly , godot , or some other js framework. Each has a benefit and a downside also.

replies.author: Fair_Simple_8813
replies.body: Thanks for the detailed breakdown. Before committing to a full rewrite, I'd try a tiny version of the same harbour scene in the alternatives, with the same assets and player count. Include loading time and those freezes in the comparison too. That would make a useful follow-up post, even if you end up sticking with the current setup.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body:
Hi, I got a serious question. Since you seem serious about your game. Why a browser game? 
From a system architecture perspective I can't see anything positive besides instant shareability. 
There are so many bottlenecks with webdev and I would choose a proper gameengine. 
I don't want to be rude, I just don't understand it. 
Enlighten me please

replies.author: First_Teach
replies.body: Hi, because our main goal is to create a game that everybody from everywhere can play and just come to chill, now the game is desinged for desktop and mobiles also, so when you open the [talewyn.org](http://talewyn.org) from the  mobile you can play the game from the mobile at the work or in the train.. and if you are going to home you can continue from your browser :)

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body:
I get that. I'm just making sure that you make an educated decision. Ai makes it very easy to choose three.js. But many ppl don't realize the limitations. 
but that's actually  where you should start the process, to see what is possible and what's not. 

Good luck
